title: Battle of the Atlantic
description: Naval campaign in World War II
wiki_lead:
The Battle of the Atlantic, the longest continuous military campaign in World War II, ran from 1939 to the defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945, covering a major part of the naval history of World War II. At its core was the Allied naval blockade of Germany, announced the day after the declaration of war, and Germany's subsequent counterblockade. The campaign peaked from mid-1940 to the end of 1943.
The Battle of the Atlantic pitted U-boats and other warships of the German Kriegsmarine (navy) and aircraft of the Luftwaffe (air force) against the Royal Navy, Royal Canadian Navy, United States Navy, and Allied merchant shipping. Convoys, coming mainly from North America and predominantly going to the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, were protected for the most part by the British and Canadian navies and air forces. These forces were aided by ships and aircraft of the United States beginning on 13 September 1941. The Germans were joined by submarines of the Italian Regia Marina (royal navy) after Germany's Axis ally Italy entered the war on 10 June 1940.
As an island country, the United Kingdom was highly dependent on imported goods. Britain required more than a million tons of imported material per week in order to survive and fight. The Battle of the Atlantic involved a tonnage war: the Allies struggled to supply Britain while the Axis targeted merchant shipping critical to the British war effort. Rationing in the United Kingdom was also used with the aim of reducing demand, by reducing wastage and increasing domestic production and equality of distribution. From 1942 onwards, the Axis also sought to prevent the build-up of Allied supplies and equipment in the UK in preparation for the invasion of occupied Europe. The defeat of the U-boat threat was a prerequisite for pushing back the Axis in western Europe. The outcome of the battle was a strategic victory for the Allies—the German tonnage war failed—but at great cost: 3,500 merchant ships and 175 warships were sunk in the Atlantic for the loss of 783 U-boats and 47 German surface warships, including 4 battleships (Bismarck, Scharnhorst, Gneisenau, and Tirpitz), 9 cruisers, 7 raiders, and 27 destroyers. This front was a main consumer of the German war effort: Germany spent more money to produce naval vessels than every type of ground vehicle combined, including tanks.
The Battle of the Atlantic has been called the "longest, largest, and most complex" naval battle in history. Starting immediately after the European war began, during the Phoney War, the battle lasted for over five years until the German surrender in May 1945. It involved thousands of ships in a theatre covering millions of square miles of ocean. The situation changed constantly, with one side or the other gaining advantage, as participating countries surrendered, joined and even changed sides in the war, and as new weapons, tactics, countermeasures and equipment were developed. The Allies gradually gained the upper hand, overcoming German surface-raiders by the end of 1942 and defeating the U-boats by mid-1943, though losses due to U-boats continued until the war's end. British prime minister Winston Churchill later wrote, "The only thing that really frightened me during the war was the U-boat peril. I was even more anxious about this battle than I had been about the glorious air fight called the 'Battle of Britain'."

Name
On 5 March 1941, the First Lord of the Admiralty, A. V. Alexander, asked Parliament for "many more ships and great numbers of men" to fight "the Battle of the Atlantic", which he compared to the Battle of France fought the previous summer. The first meeting of the Cabinet's "Battle of the Atlantic Committee" was on 19 March. Churchill claimed to have coined the phrase "Battle of the Atlantic" shortly before Alexander's speech, but there are several examples of earlier usage.

grok_lead: The Battle of the Atlantic was the longest continuous military campaign of World War II, spanning from 3 September 1939 to the defeat of Nazi Germany in May 1945, and pitting the Axis powersâprimarily Nazi Germany's Kriegsmarine U-boat force, surface raiders, and Luftwaffe aircraftâagainst the Allied navies and merchant shipping of Britain, the United States, Canada, and other nations in a desperate struggle for control of transatlantic supply lines. The campaign's core objective for Germany, initiated immediately after the invasion of Poland, was to sever Britain's lifeline by sinking merchant vessels carrying vital food, fuel, raw materials, and troops across the Atlantic, thereby starving the island nation into submission and preventing the buildup of Allied forces for a potential European invasion. In response, the Allies, led initially by the Royal Navy and later bolstered by the U.S. Navy following America's entry into the war in December 1941, organized merchant ships into defended convoys escorted by destroyers, corvettes, and aircraft, employing tactics that evolved from early vulnerabilities to sophisticated anti-submarine warfare. The battle extended across the entire Atlantic Ocean, including the North Atlantic, the U.S. East Coast (targeted in Germany's Operation Drumbeat in early 1942), the Gulf of Mexico, and even the South Atlantic after Brazil's declaration of war on Germany in August 1942. Throughout the conflict, German U-boats sank approximately 3,500 Allied merchant ships totaling 14.5 million gross tons, along with 175 warships, resulting in the loss of over 72,000 Allied merchant seamen and naval personnel, while the Kriegsmarine suffered the destruction of 783 U-boats and around 30,000 submariners. The tide turned decisively in favor of the Allies by mid-1943, thanks to breakthroughs such as the cracking of German Enigma codes by British intelligence at Bletchley Park, the widespread deployment of radar and sonar-equipped escorts, the introduction of long-range aircraft and escort carriers like the USS Santee, and improved convoy coordination that outpaced U-boat production and tactics. This victory ensured the uninterrupted flow of Lend-Lease supplies to Britain and the Soviet Union, enabling the mounting of major offensives including the D-Day invasion of Normandy in 1944. The Battle of the Atlantic's historical significance lies in its role as the pivotal naval struggle of the war, described by Winston Churchill as the "only thing that ever really frightened me during the war," as its outcome determined whether the Allies could sustain their global effort against the Axis powers. It drove innovations in naval technology, intelligence, and logistics that shaped modern warfare, while underscoring the human cost of attrition in an unforgiving oceanic theater.
